newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Peugeot UK workers vote for strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Peugeot UK workers vote for strike.

text.p: British workers at French car-maker PSA Peugeot raised the spectre of an all-out strike on Wednesday after workers voted overwhelmingly in favour of striking in protest against pay and conditions.
Union bosses at Transport and General (T&G), the main trade union involved, said 1,720 workers at the Peugeot Motor Co's Coventry plant had backed strike action, with 363 against.
In a vote on other forms of industrial action, 1,848 were in favour, with 243 against.
Peugeot employs around 3,000 workers in Coventry, its main British production facility which turned out 85,000 vehicles in 1996.
Both sides said they were now going to digest the results before deciding their next step.

Tony Woodley, national secretary for the motor industry at the T&G said the move to test worker support for all-out strike was a reflection of "mounting frustration" over the last year over pay and conditions.
But union leaders left the door ajar for possible conciliation, with Woodley stating "Negotiation is better than confrontation, but it takes two to negotiate."
Chris Edwards, spokesman for Peugeot at Coventry, told Reuters "We are trying to clarify the situation before we do anything."

The vote backing a strike means unions can now call for industrial action if talks with Peugeot fail. The strike ballot was triggered by a dispute over pay and conditions, with unions accusing Peugeot of trying to introduce longer shifts and refusing to bring pay in line with other manufacturers.
Peugeot refused to comment on the root of the row, but said negotiations had been ongoing between the two sides since December.
Peugeot's British plant supplies the local and export market and has just under eight percent of the market in Britain and seven percent in Europe.
Coventry is one of three Peugeot production facilities in Europe, with the other two in Spain and France with capacity of 210,000 cars and 306,000, respectively.
Charles Young, director of research at LMC International, the motor industry analyst, said Coventry was "a low production and antiquated plant."
"If there was a strike, I don't think Peugeot would have much trouble transferring capacity elsewhere," Young said.

The unions' demand for more money also comes at a time when the European market is sluggish, with the French market in particularly deep recession after government incentives to buy new cars ended in 1996 leading to a collapse in demand.
Young said Peugeot did not have much money to splash around even if it did face strike threats.
"The unions are in a weak position. They are threatening to strike but it's not as if customers are falling over themselves to buy Peugeot cars."

The industry is facing a stormy time in the rest of Europe as well. Fellow French car maker Renault SA has ignited anger at home with plans to axe 2,764 jobs in France on top of a plant closure in Belgium.
Ford Motor Co incurred similar wrath in Britain earlier this year when it threatened to close its Halewood plant in north-east England to cut mounting European losses.
But it has since clinched agreement with unions, averted a British strike and has hinted it is close to receiving a major subsidy from the British government to keep Halewood running.
